{{Short description|Concept in probability theory}}
[[File:Markov Inequality.svg|thumb|300px|right|Markov's inequality gives an upper bound for the measure of the set (indicated in red) where <math>f(x)</math> exceeds a given level <math>\varepsilon</math>. The bound combines the level <math>\varepsilon</math> with the average value of <math>f</math>.]]
In [[probability theory]], '''Markov's inequality''' gives an [[upper bound]] on the [[probability]] that a [[non-negative]] [[random variable]] is greater than or equal to some positive [[Constant (mathematics)|constant]]. Markov's inequality is tight in the sense that for each chosen positive constant, there exists a random variable such that the inequality is in fact an equality.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Huber |first=Mark |date=2019-11-26 |title=Halving the Bounds for the Markov, Chebyshev, and Chernoff Inequalities Using Smoothing |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00029890.2019.1656484 |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |language=en |volume=126 |issue=10 |pages=915–927 |doi=10.1080/00029890.2019.1656484 |issn=0002-9890|arxiv=1803.06361 }}</ref>

It is named after the Russian mathematician [[Andrey Markov]], although it appeared earlier in the work of [[Pafnuty Chebyshev]] (Markov's teacher), and many sources, especially in [[Mathematical analysis|analysis]], refer to it as Chebyshev's inequality (sometimes, calling it the first Chebyshev inequality, while referring to [[Chebyshev's inequality]] as the second Chebyshev inequality) or [[Irénée-Jules Bienaymé|Bienaymé]]'s inequality.

Markov's inequality (and other similar inequalities) relate probabilities to [[expected value|expectation]]s, and provide (frequently loose but still useful) bounds for the [[cumulative distribution function]] of a random variable. [[Michael Mitzenmacher|Mitzenmacher]] and [[Eli Upfal|Upfal]] note that Markov's inequality "is often too weak to yield useful results, but it is still a fundamental tool in developing more sophisticated bounds".

Markov's inequality can also be used to upper bound the expectation of a non-negative random variable in terms of its distribution function.

==Statement==
If {{mvar|X}} is a nonnegative random variable and {{math|''a''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0}}, then the probability
that {{mvar|X}} is at least {{mvar|a}} is at most the expectation of {{mvar|X}} divided by {{mvar|a}}:<ref name=":0" />

:<math>\operatorname{P}(X \geq a) \leq \frac{\operatorname{E}(X)}{a}.</math>

When <math>\operatorname{E}(X) > 0</math>, we can take <math> a = \tilde{a} \cdot \operatorname{E}(X) </math> for <math> \tilde{a} > 0 </math> to rewrite the previous inequality as

:<math>\operatorname{P}(X \geq \tilde{a} \cdot \operatorname{E}(X)) \leq \frac{1}{\tilde{a}}.</math>

In the language of [[measure theory]], Markov's inequality states that if {{math|(''X'',&nbsp;Σ,&nbsp;''μ'')}} is a [[Measure (mathematics)|measure space]], <math>f</math> is a [[measurable function|measurable]] [[extended real number line|extended real]]-valued function, and {{math|''&epsilon;'' > 0}}, then

:<math> \mu(\{x\in X:|f(x)|\geq \varepsilon \}) \leq \frac 1 \varepsilon \int_X |f|\,d\mu.</math>

This measure-theoretic definition is sometimes referred to as [[Chebyshev's inequality]].<ref>{{citation| author1-first= E. M. | author1-last= Stein| author2-first=R. | author2-last=Shakarchi | author1-link= Elias M. Stein | title=Real Analysis |  series=[[Princeton Lectures in Analysis]] | volume=3 | edition= 1st | year= 2005| page= 91}}.</ref>



===Extended version for nondecreasing functions===
If {{mvar|&phi;}} is a nondecreasing nonnegative function, {{mvar|X}} is a (not necessarily nonnegative) random variable, and {{math|''&phi;''(''a'') > 0}}, then<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Lin |first=Zhengyan |title=Probability inequalities |publisher=Springer |year=2010 |pages=52}}</ref>

:<math>\operatorname P (X \ge a) \le \frac{\operatorname E(\varphi(X))}{\varphi(a)}.</math>

An immediate corollary, using higher moments of {{mvar|X}} supported on values larger than 0, is

:<math>\operatorname P (|X| \ge a) \le \frac{\operatorname E(|X|^n)}{a^n}.</math>

The respective measure-theoretic versions are
:<math>\mu(\{x \in X : |f(x)| \geq \varepsilon\}) \leq \frac{1}{\varphi(\varepsilon)} \int_X \varphi(|f|).</math>
and
:<math>\mu(\{x \in X : |f(x)| \geq \varepsilon\}) \leq \frac{1}{\varepsilon^p} \int_X |f|^p = \frac{1}{\varepsilon^p} \|f\|_{L^p}^p.</math>
Where <math>\|\cdot\|_{L^p}</math> denotes the [[Lp norm]].

===The uniformly randomized Markov's inequality===

If {{mvar|X}} is a nonnegative random variable and {{math|''a''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0}}, and  {{mvar|U}} is a uniformly distributed random variable on <math>[0,1]</math> that is independent of  {{mvar|X}}, then<ref>{{citation| author1-first= Aaditya | author1-last= Ramdas| author2-first=Tudor | author2-last=Manole | title = Randomized and Exchangeable Improvements of Markov's, Chebyshev's and Chernoff's Inequalities | date= 2023| arxiv=2304.02611}}.</ref>

:<math>\operatorname{P}(X \geq Ua) \leq \frac{\operatorname{E}(X)}{a}.</math>

Since {{mvar|U}} is almost surely smaller than one, this bound is strictly stronger than Markov's inequality. Remarkably, {{mvar|U}} cannot be replaced by any constant smaller than one, meaning that deterministic improvements to Markov's inequality cannot exist in general. While Markov's inequality holds with equality for distributions supported on <math>\{0,a\}</math>, the above randomized variant holds with equality for any distribution that is bounded on <math>[0,a]</math>.

==Proofs==
We begin with the case for discrete random variables.

===Discrete case===
We now provide a proof for the special case when <math>X</math> is a discrete random variable which only takes on non-negative integer values. 

<math>
E[X] = \sum_{i} i\,P(X=i)
\;\geq\; \sum_{i \geq a} i\,P(X=i)
\;\geq\; \sum_{i \geq a} a\,P(X=i)
= a \sum_{i \geq a} P(X=i)
= a\,P(X \geq a)
</math> 

Now we consider continuous random variables too. We separate the case in which the measure space is a probability space from the more general case because the probability case is more accessible for the general reader.

===Intuition===
<math>\operatorname{E}(X) = \operatorname{P}(X < a)\cdot \operatorname{E}(X|X<a) + \operatorname{P}(X \geq a)\cdot \operatorname{E}(X|X\geq a)</math> where <math>\operatorname{E}(X|X<a)</math> is larger than or equal to 0 as the random variable <math>X</math> is non-negative and <math>\operatorname{E}(X|X\geq a)</math> is larger than or equal to <math>a</math> because the conditional expectation only takes into account of values larger than or equal to <math>a</math> which r.v. <math>X</math> can take.

'''Property 1:''' <math>\operatorname{P}(X < a) \cdot \operatorname{E}(X \mid X < a) \geq 0</math>

Given a non-negative random variable <math>X</math>, the conditional expectation <math>\operatorname{E}(X \mid X < a) \geq 0</math> because <math>X \geq 0</math>. Also, probabilities are always non-negative, i.e., <math>\operatorname{P}(X < a) \geq 0</math>. Thus, the product:

<math>\operatorname{P}(X < a) \cdot \operatorname{E}(X \mid X < a) \geq 0</math>.

This is intuitive since conditioning on <math> X < a </math> still results in non-negative values, ensuring the product remains non-negative.

'''Property 2:''' <math>\operatorname{P}(X \geq a) \cdot \operatorname{E}(X \mid X \geq a) \geq a \cdot \operatorname{P}(X \geq a) </math>

For <math> X \geq a </math>, the expected value given <math> X \geq a</math> is at least <math> a. \operatorname{E}(X \mid X \geq a) \geq a </math>. Multiplying both sides by <math> \operatorname{P}(X \geq a) </math>, we get:

<math>\operatorname{P}(X \geq a) \cdot \operatorname{E}(X \mid X \geq a) \geq a \cdot \operatorname{P}(X \geq a)</math>.

This is intuitive since all values considered are at least <math>a</math>, making their average also greater than or equal to <math>a</math>.

Hence intuitively, <math>\operatorname{E}(X)\geq \operatorname{P}(X \geq a)\cdot \operatorname{E}(X|X\geq a)\geq a \cdot \operatorname{P}(X\geq a)</math>, which directly leads to <math>\operatorname{P}(X\geq a)\leq \frac{\operatorname{E}(X)}{a}</math>.

===Probability-theoretic proof===
'''Method 1:'''
From the definition of expectation: 
:<math>\operatorname{E}(X)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} xf(x) \, dx</math>

However, <math>X</math> is a non-negative random variable thus,  
:<math>\operatorname{E}(X)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty xf(x) \, dx = \int_0^\infty xf(x) \, dx </math>

From this we can derive, 
:<math>\operatorname{E}(X)=\int_0^a xf(x) \, dx + \int_a^\infty xf(x) \, dx \ge  \int_a^\infty xf(x) \, dx \ge\int_a^\infty af(x) \, dx = a\int_a^\infty f(x) \, dx= a \operatorname{Pr}(X \ge a)</math>

From here, dividing through by <math>a</math> allows us to see that 

:<math>\Pr(X \ge a) \le \operatorname{E}(X)/a</math>

'''Method 2:'''
For any event <math>E</math>, let <math>I_E</math> be the indicator random variable of <math> E </math>, that is, <math>I_E=1</math> if <math>E</math> occurs and <math>I_E=0</math> otherwise.

Using this notation, we have <math>I_{(X\geq a)}=1</math> if the event <math>X\geq a</math> occurs, and <math>I_{(X\geq a)}=0</math> if <math>X<a</math>.  Then, given <math>a>0</math>,

:<math>aI_{(X \geq a)} \leq X</math>

which is clear if we consider the two possible values of <math>X\geq a</math>.  If <math>X<a</math>, then <math>I_{(X\geq a)}=0</math>, and so <math>a I_{(X\geq a)}=0\leq X</math>.  Otherwise, we have <math>X\geq a</math>, for which <math>I_{X\geq a}=1</math> and so <math>aI_{X\geq a}=a\leq X</math>.

Since <math>\operatorname{E}</math> is a monotonically increasing function, taking expectation of both sides of an inequality cannot reverse it. Therefore,

:<math>\operatorname{E}(aI_{(X \geq a)}) \leq \operatorname{E}(X).</math>

Now, using linearity of expectations, the left side of this inequality is the same as

:<math>a\operatorname{E}(I_{(X \geq a)}) = a(1\cdot\operatorname{P}(X \geq a) + 0\cdot\operatorname{P}(X < a)) = a\operatorname{P}(X \geq a).</math>

Thus we have

:<math>a\operatorname{P}(X \geq a) \leq \operatorname{E}(X)</math>

and since ''a''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0, we can divide both sides by&nbsp;''a''.

===Measure-theoretic proof===
We may assume that the function <math>f</math> is non-negative, since only its absolute value enters in the equation. Now, consider the real-valued function ''s'' on ''X'' given by

:<math>
s(x) =
\begin{cases}
  \varepsilon, & \text{if } f(x) \geq \varepsilon  \\
  0, & \text{if } f(x) < \varepsilon
\end{cases}
</math>

Then <math>0\leq s(x)\leq f(x)</math>. By the definition of the [[Lebesgue integral]]

:<math>
\int_X f(x) \, d\mu \geq \int_X s(x) \, d \mu = \varepsilon \mu( \{ x\in X : \, f(x) \geq \varepsilon \} )
</math>

and since <math>\varepsilon >0 </math>, both sides can be divided by <math>\varepsilon</math>, obtaining

:<math>\mu(\{x\in X : \, f(x) \geq \varepsilon \}) \leq {1\over \varepsilon }\int_X f \,d\mu.</math>

The extended version may be proved in the same fashion:
:<math> \varphi(\varepsilon) \cdot \mu(\{x \in X : |f(x)| \geq \varepsilon\}) = \int_{\{x \in X : |f(x)| \geq \varepsilon\}} \varphi(\varepsilon)\,d\mu \leq \int_{\{x \in X : |f(x)| \geq \varepsilon\}} \varphi(|f|)\,d\mu \leq \int_X \varphi(|f|)\,d\mu. </math>
Diving through by <math>\varphi(\varepsilon)</math> yields the result:
:<math> \mu(\{x\in X : \, |f(x)| \geq \varepsilon \}) \leq {1\over \varphi(\varepsilon) }\int_X \varphi(|f|) \,d\mu. </math>

=== Chebyshev's inequality ===
[[Chebyshev's inequality]] uses the [[variance]] to bound the probability that a random variable deviates far from the mean. Specifically, 

:<math>\operatorname{P}(|X-\operatorname{E}(X)| \geq a) \leq \frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{a^2},</math>

for any {{math|''a'' > 0}}.<ref name=":1" /> Here {{math|Var(''X'')}} is the [[variance]] of X, defined as:

:<math> \operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{E}[(X - \operatorname{E}(X) )^2]. </math>

Chebyshev's inequality follows from Markov's inequality by considering the random variable

: <math> (X - \operatorname{E}(X))^2 </math>

and the constant <math>a^2,</math> for which Markov's inequality reads

: <math> \operatorname{P}( (X - \operatorname{E}(X))^2 \ge a^2) \le \frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{a^2}.</math>

This argument can be summarized (where "MI" indicates use of Markov's inequality):

:<math>\operatorname{P}(|X-\operatorname{E}(X)| \geq a) = 
\operatorname{P}\left((X-\operatorname{E}(X))^2 \geq a^2\right) \,\overset{\underset{\mathrm{MI}}{}}{\leq}\, 
\frac {\operatorname{E} \left( (X-\operatorname{E}(X))^2 \right)}{a^2} =
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{a^2}.</math>

\operatorname{P}(M \npreceq A) \leq \operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname E (M) A^{-1})

==Examples==

=== Example 1: Income distribution in populations ===
Assuming no income is negative, Markov's inequality shows that no more than 10% (1/10) of the population can have more than 10 times the average income.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Ross |first=Kevin |url=https://bookdown.org/kevin_davisross/probsim-book/probability-inequalitlies.html |title=5.4 Probability inequalitlies {{!}} An Introduction to Probability and Simulation}}</ref>

=== Example 2: Distribution of test scores ===
Another simple example is as follows: Andrew makes 4 mistakes on average on his Statistics course tests. The best upper bound on the probability that Andrew will make at least 10 mistakes is 0.4 as <math>\operatorname{P}(X \geq 10) \leq   \frac{\operatorname{E}(X)}{\alpha} = \frac{4}{10}.</math> Note that Andrew might do exactly 10 mistakes with probability 0.4 and make no mistakes with probability 0.6; the expectation is exactly 4 mistakes.

=== Example 3: Heads in a sequence of coin flips ===
We want to find the probability of finding more than <math>3n/4</math> heads in a sequence of <math>n</math> coin flips. Since the coin flips form a [[binomial distribution]], the expected number of heads is <math>np = \frac{n}{2}</math>, by Markov's inequality it follows that <math>\Pr(X \geq 3n/4) \leq \frac{n/2}{3n/4} = 2/3</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mitzenmacher |first=Michael |title=Probability and computing: randomized algorithms and probabilistic analysis |last2=Upfal |first2=Eli |date=2005 |publisher=Cambridge university press |isbn=978-0-521-83540-4 |location=Cambridge}}</ref>
